key_insight: Automated nasalization measures—Nasal Cognate Distinctiveness (NCD) and nasal posterior probability (NPP)—tracked hypernasality severity in motor speech disorders and performed similarly for identifying clinically meaningful hypernasality.
clinical_relevance: These tools could help provide objective, scalable support for assessing hypernasality in speech-language evaluation, especially when human ratings are needed at larger scale or over time.
method: Analyzed sentence-level speech from 561 participants (374 controls, 187 with motor speech disorders).
Computed NCD for voiceless stops (/p/, /t/, /k/) and NPP from a phonological feature-based neural network across stops, consonants, and vowels.
Compared measures with clinician-rated hypernasality using mixed-effects models, correlations, ROC analyses, and test-retest reliability testing.
evidence_signal: Across measures, higher hypernasality was linked to lower NCD and higher NPP, with ROC performance showing moderate-to-good discrimination (e.g., NCD AUC 0.796, NPP AUC 0.730 for absent vs present hypernasality; consonant/vowel NPP AUC 0.853).
watch_item: Performance was measured in a research cohort, so real-world deployment will need validation across speakers, recording conditions, and clinical settings, plus attention to small test-retest changes near the MDC threshold.
paper_title: Automated Assessment of Hypernasality in Motor Speech Disorders Using Nasal Cognate Distinctiveness and Nasal Posterior Probability
